utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number, IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Brdjanin, good afternoon to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And General Talic, can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. These -- Madam Registrar, if you could find them a place, because, for example, I'm not seeing Mr. Trbojevic, because -- they obstruct the view. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Joanna Korner, assisted by Hasan Younis, case manager. Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman along with Marela Jevtovic. As I reported to you last week, Mr. Trbojevic will be absent this week in Banja Luka. And that's probably why you don't see him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Appearances for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic and Natasha Ivanovic-Fauveau for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good afternoon to you. So, as we agreed, the first half hour to be dedicated to the admissibility or objections that are being raised supposedly by the Defence on the -- to the video. I got a video this morning which I thought it was it, but it had nothing to do with the case. It had to do with the Mrdza or Mrdzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I have two other short matters to deal with, but I think I'll leave them till afterwards. Your Honours, thanks to real commitment by members of the language staff who are not really part of the investigation over the weekend, we've had prepared a transcript in both -- well, in B/C/S originally, translated into English. Now, Your Honour, Mr. Ackerman objected to Your Honours seeing the transcript. I do not in all conscience understand how an argument against admissibility can be mounted unless Your Honours know what on earth everybody is talking about. So Your Honours, my application this morning -- this afternoon is that Your Honours now get a copy of the transcript and that if necessary you can watch the video, which is available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, whoever it was that did -- made the effort to get this transcript prepared in the short time involved should be commended I think by all of us. It's a remarkable job. The second thing: I have been in consultation with counsel for General Talic. We have both had an opportunity to both view the tape and to look at the transcript. And at this point our objection is limited to those portions of the tape which contain the voice of persons who are not identified, and specifically there are significant portions of the tape where there's a voiceover done by some unidentified commentator, and we cannot identify who that person is, and therefore we could not -- we could neither interview nor call that person for testimony here. The other people are people who we have been able to identify and we think probably the tape is appropriate with regard to those people who were chief of police, part of the Crisis Staff, things like that in Kljuc at the time. So our objection is limited to the unidentified voices that appear on the tape.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the first application was that Your Honours should all be given copies of the transcript, because the unidentified voices so-called by Mr. Ackerman are in fact clearly a television commentator, and it is as much the commentary to this tape that we say is relevant and admissible for what we say is, as Mr. Ackerman pointed out yesterday -- Friday, propaganda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was this -- may I ask, what is this video exactly? What -- is it a TV documentary or what?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's -- it appears to be a programme that went out on, it is thought, by Mr. Filipovic, Banja Luka Television. He can't say who taped it or when it was, but he can identify a lot of the places, the people, and the like. And he actually gets a special mention on the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we verify if Mr. Filipovic is in a position to identify the commentator? Because if it's a local production, I mean, I'm -- looking at this coming from a small place, a small country, where normally if you are familiar with -- you will be able to identify the commentator very easily, if there are only two or three local stations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it may well be. I don't know. And he's not here at the moment I don't think. Well, he may have been brought here. But Your Honour, in our submission, it wouldn't -- it would of course be added weight. But it wouldn't matter whether or not he could identify the commentator. But Your Honour, I don't know whether Mr. Ackerman or Mr. Zecevic maintain their objection to Your Honours having a copy of the transcript at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You realise, Mr. Ackerman, that very much -- we very much need to see -- have something in our hands before we can really say --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think you should see it, because I think it will help you understand what our objection is about. There is just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How long is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's 20 pages in the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The video recording itself, how long is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I'm afraid to say I haven't actually timed it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think it's about --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's about 40 minutes, I think, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: About 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But I'm cutting out -- the first 20 minutes whoever it was pointed out is all about some bullfight. So I'd say all in all the relevant part is about 20 minutes. I mean, I've set up a particular video to start at that part. Well, would the -- would the answer be -- as the objection really only relates now to what is the voiceover of the commentator, if Your Honours were to take the transcript now and perhaps read through it and we can -- I think it will be a much shorter -- and indeed we can have Mr. Filipovic in at quarter to 3.00 and ask him that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's what -- Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm just wondering if it makes sense for you to do that if Mr. Filipovic is here, we could go ahead and start and just save using the tape or any part of it until tomorrow, and that would give you more time to look at the transcript and the tape if you wanted that additional time, rather than interrupt testimony. But that will be up to you, the way you want to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That seems -- it makes sense to me, provided that it is anticipated to go into tomorrow with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- Mr. Filipovic will undoubtedly be going into tomorrow, probably into Wednesday, probably into Wednesday, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Then I think we can read this at home this evening and then we'll discuss it tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, then, Your Honour, I'm going to ask that Your Honours be handed now copies of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think we need the video recording for the time being, because it doesn't make sense looking at it too, apart from these transcripts. So basically --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, unless --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it that this is the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Unless you'd like to see the bullfight, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not exactly my -- I have got strong reservations about that sport, if you call it a sport.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's not the typical man fights bull. It's bull fights bull, which is a different variation of that whole process than I've ever seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's one of the cruelest -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, then can I move to two other matters. Could we go into private session for the first, because it relates to witness protection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are just two matters that remain, both of which really relate to motions that were put in. The first is the application to 92 bis, a number of the Kljuc witnesses. I was going to say that Kljuc will be quite fast. This witness and another one will be long, because they're going to deal with documents. But the rest will be very short. It's all crime base. And we anticipate starting Prijedor towards the end of September. So we'd like to know if Your Honours would be kind enough, whether we can have the ruling on Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes. This morning, actually -- I haven't had time to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I haven't had time to discuss, but the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So basically I worked on the basis of the discussions that we had had between ourselves and also with our legal staff on 92 bis. There were a few addenda to be made in the decision to make it reflect the various opinions and have a unanimous decision. And I take it that should -- yeah, I should have it on my desk tomorrow morning for signature, and that should keep you all very happy. So that's -- the protective measures one also was delayed precisely because I wanted to air my -- our concerns about this risk assessment business. However, more or less we are in a position to hand down the judgement -- the decision any time. So -- but I understand that you -- 92 bis is perhaps more urgent because Prijedor ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, as Your Honour knows, a number of the witnesses already received protective measures from not one but two or three other cases, so it may be that that's a simpler --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Protective measures. I also asked for my staff to make a -- particularly with regard to Prijedor -- to make a comparative study with those witnesses that are common to both Stakic and this case that had asked for and were afforded, accorded protective measures. There are one or two that had not asked for protective measures in Stakic or were not produced in Stakic and produced as witnesses in this case. So but it's something that is in hand. So it's -- I don't think it's going to cause us any problems. We will need to sit down and go through it, make sure that it -- there is agreement on each and every part of that decision. And we can hand it down pretty soon.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, then the last matter is Mr. Shellow's response to our analysis of straightforward pure law on contempt and misconduct. Your Honour will recall last week when it was raised Your Honours hadn't had a chance to read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have read it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I said that if Your Honours were going to take -- as it's an argument on the fact, then it may well be that we should respond, because it's not in fact what was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, there are two options. We either expunge it from the records straight away, which is the temptation that I have, and we would leave it at that. The other alternative is obviously what you are suggesting now. We haven't reached a decision on whether to expunge it or not because we did not discuss it again. We discussed it very briefly last week. I suppose before we tell you yes, before we give you the green light for a reply, we better decide whether to keep it in the records or expunge it straight away.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't actually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because it's definitely beyond what was --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I mean -- well I'm not going to go into what Mr. Shellow thought he was doing. But in any event, Your Honours will recall that when this procedure first came up, I expressed my reservations about -- we were actually in one sense pre-judging something, because this is an argument on everything. All I can say is we would be unhappy about having to put a reply into this because we would be in a sense arguing a matter which may well be dealt with by another branch of this Tribunal and not Your Honours. And as I say, it's always been a bit difficult to work out what Mr. Shellow's -- what the procedure which allowed Mr. Shellow to address Your Honours actually was. So Your Honours, I'm merely raising it. But if Your Honours intended to take it into account in making your decision as to whether or not to institute either proceedings for contempt or misconduct, then I think Your Honours, it would only be right that we should ask for the right to reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But in all fairness, we haven't discussed it again. So I think we will need to postpone our decision after we have discussed it between us. There is another option, of course, and that is returning everything to Mr. Shellow, telling him to re-file -- re-file it within the terms of what we had agreed should be the parameters of the discussion. That is another -- another way of approaching it. But --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. Because in fact he doesn't refer to any authorities anywhere --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. But please do accept my apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We were supposed to have a meeting, the three of us, last week, which I had to cancel at the last minute because of something urgent that came up. So we haven't had a time to meet --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That all right, Your Honour. I just saw it lying there, so I thought I'd raise it gone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Ready to --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since Ms. Korner has just said that she hopes to start with the Prijedor municipality at the end of September, I would like to ask her in public so she can disclose us the list of witnesses for Prijedor and the List of Documents, because it is a municipality which is by all means the largest ones, and we won't have the time if we receive the list at the last minute, we won't be able to deal with the trial and to file all the documents at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... we would I think transmit the List of Documents plus their definitive -- as far as Prijedor ever is definitive -- list of witnesses by the end of this week. Your Honour, I was going to raise it at a later stage, but I agree with Mr. Ackerman that I think if Your Honour gives two days on top of the time off we're already having -- I can't remember when the first break is now. Is it the last week in September?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it's 27 -- 29th of September.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, then, Your Honour, I think it might be sensible if all parties were agreed, if Your Honours were to add on two further days the following week for -- but with the provisor that all parties have to get together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usually the way I do it, Ms. Korner, is that I usually leave it in the hands of the parties to agree on the dates.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There being flexibility on our parts. In other words we don't have any other commitments ourselves except the work that we have in this Tribunal. So basically if you try and sit round the table and tell us what you -- what you require, what you want, we will be in a position to accommodate you --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Or Your Honour, it may even be the two days before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly whichever. Whether you want the two days before, or the two days after, it doesn't really make a difference to us because we are here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's only -- Mr. Ackerman wants to go to Texas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No. If we're talking about Prijedor, and we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The other question that arises: We have been provided recently with what appears to be maybe a few thousand pages of transcript of testimony from the Stakic case. And I don't know if the Prosecutor is having those translated into the language of the accused or intends to provide us with tapes. But one or the other I would suggest ought to be done with as much dispatch as possible so that the accused will have an opportunity to see what it is these witnesses have said in the Stakic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Prijedor is a very important municipality. It's make it or break it, in my opinion, Prijedor. After Prijedor we should all know more or less what the situation looks like on the horizontal. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's -- Kotor Varos, Your Honour, which -- I agree that in between there are a number of smaller municipalities. But Kotor Varos is a major municipality. And Bosanski Novi is not exactly small.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But anyway please do take Prijedor because I envisage it's going to take us a long time to start with. And it's not an easy -- from what I know, what I have followed from the Stakic case, it's not an easy municipality at all. It's -- it will be a difficult one. So if you can sort of thrash these things amongst yourselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, certainly I will. I know that I've been reminded by Mr. Younis that a request was made to the registry by Ms. Gustin sometime ago for the tapes, I think before she left on her summer holiday so we'll make inquiries to what's happening both that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the answer is no, we won't be trying get it translated. And Your Honour, one of the things we discussed, and I hope we can discuss again with the Defence, is that the shortest way of asking witnesses to testify who have already testified at least once and in some cases twice and three times - one of them Mr. Sejmenovic - this will be his fifth testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is it. I mean, I would prefer you to sit down round a table and come to some kind of agreement, because we -- we can hear each and every witness viva voce in chief and then in cross, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If there is an easier way out ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: My suggestion, and I'll leave it now, because as I say, I think we need to discuss this with the witness and maybe with Your Honours -- is that where there is somebody that has really testified on a number of occasions, that his prior transcripts or some portion become the major part of his evidence in chief but with obviously a few additional questions on -- concentrating on the really important parts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Can we bring the witness in. He is open session, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will be continuing with your testimony today. And before you do so, may I kindly ask you to repeat your solemn declaration to tell us the truth once more, please. Thank you. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Ms. Korner. Examined by Ms. Korner: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, before we continue with your description of the events in Kljuc, can I just ask you this: The videotape that you brought with you and which you've watched, there's apparently a television commentator. Did you by any chance know who that television commentator is?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know his name, but at the end of the tape - I think it's there - and his face appears and he's bald. It's possible to recognise the speaker. The speaker can be identified. I can point him out to you on the videotape.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. We'll -- we'll deal with it when we come to the tape then. All right. Mr. Filipovic, when we broke on Friday, we had just looked at a document that your -- a letter that your brother had been sent. And I want to move on from there to really the next document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Forgive me one moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I think you mentioned in your evidence on Friday that it was the takeover or the inability to receive television programmes from Sarajevo but in fact from Serbia that increased ethnic tensions in Kljuc. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'd now like you to have a look, please, at a document that was issued by the MBO on the 1st of August, 1991, Exhibit P856.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which will be behind divider 14 in volume 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Filipovic, do you remember a document being issued by -- on the 1st of August? In fact, it's stamped and it's got a signature. Was it your brother's signature?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And complaining that the -- well, in fact, "The pirate-like infiltration of the frequencies of Sarajevo Television's second channel, the employees of the phantom Krajina television introduced Mitel to our homes and prevented us from following Sarajevo TV's regular programme."

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it goes on to complain, I don't think we need to read all of it. The second paragraph: "We who know what media darkness is, do not need Serbian information blindness. We want to see and hear with our own eyes and ears what is happening in the country called Bosnia, in the country that once was and we hope today is still Yugoslavia. We do not need the information bulletins of Milosevic's commissars such as Mitevic or his successor Vico. We want objective information and not selected news." Who would have written this type of communication? Would it have been written by your brother himself?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He wrote them. And the reason for writing this official note is that after the break-in -- the vandalistic break-in of the then-JNA -- I think it was the JNA, because they were wearing uniforms. They entered the repeater at Kozara and redirected the second programme of Sarajevo television, so that we citizens from Bosanska Krajina were only able to watch the first programme of Sarajevo Television and the second programme of Belgrade Television. And in my statement earlier on I said that the second problem of Belgrade Television was that -- the second programme of Belgrade Television was such a programme that an ordinary person who wasn't filled with nationalist hatred and intolerance, in a very short period of time such a man would have been turned into a man who hated other peoples and who hated his fellow citizens. And this was intolerable. On several occasions we appealed to Sarajevo Television. However, Sarajevo Television was not in a position to do anything. It was helpless.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You can put that document away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you also told us on Friday that there was an objection to the Kljuc municipality becoming part of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. And I'd like you to have a look, please, at the next document in the bundle, P857, dated the 17th of September, 1991 I should say. Now, again, was this a document issued by the MBO? And on this occasion was it signed by you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. This document, among other things, relates to the event when my late brother, Omer Filipovic, was called to go and join the reserve JNA forces. We were surprised and we wondered why. It was only so that -- why should Omer Filipovic alone get a call to join the reservists and why not other leaders of other political parties? Because in Kljuc others and the SDS in particular were bothered by Omer Filipovic, because given his advanced, progressive ideas, he made it impossible for the SDS and the radical party of the SDS to do what they wanted to do. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to this monologue. The question was: Was it signed by you? The answer was yes, and that should have ended it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In fact, Your Honour, I was going on because one can see clear through reference to this part of the document. So I -- he's pre -- jumped the gun, as it were, but I was going to ask about it anyhow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That solves it. Mr. Ackerman's objection is sustained. But of course you're free to ask the question and he can continue on from where he left. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, can I please remind you, I know it's difficult, you've had a nice weekend, I hope. But if you can just answer the question I asked and I'll be asking some other questions and maybe that will cover what you want to say.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Can we just look at the beginning part of the document and then we'll come to the part that deals with your brother. It's dated the 17th of September, 1991, and you're providing information to the public.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, this came from the Radio Kljuc collection, as it were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "The proclamation of the so-called Autonomous Region of Krajina by the Serbian Democratic Party is just the latest "principled" move in the unprincipled policy of this party. It is a principled move in the sense that it continues the party's violent, unprincipled policy, combined with ultimatums and dictates and supported with weapons. And it is an unprincipled policy because it demands and takes but does not give; because its proponents are against the abuse of ethnic domination but they themselves abuse it," and so on and so forth. What was the reference in that first sentence "Combined with ultimatums and dictates and supported with weapons"? What were you referring to there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can remember, all I can say is that I wanted to say that at the time -- the only thing -- whatever the SDS had on its mind went through in Kljuc. So the other parties, whatever our objectives were and whatever we attempted to do, we didn't succeed in doing this because we were in the minority and we weren't in power. And this relates to this aspect. It would be implemented -- a decision would be implemented if the SDS needed to implement something. This would be done. An ultimatum would be issued. They would simply threaten not to provide salaries or other things. So they were those who decided everything. And if we go back 10 or 12 years I can see that we were -- we just tried to fight for ourselves and all we could do was write things down, scribble.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can we look, then, please further down the page. You mention in the third paragraph the occupation of the television relay station on Mount Kozara, which you've already referred to. Then you refer to a man named Martic being arrested. The Court may remember. But just, Mr. Filipovic, can you remind us who Martic was.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Martic was an army commander in the Serbian Autonomous Region in Croatian Krajina. And he was arrested in Bosnia-Herzegovina near Bosanska Krupa, and then there were big demonstrations of SDS members and he was released.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then at the bottom of the page you say this: "We want Yugoslavia, and we want it to be based on our agreement. We recognise no Autonomous Region of Krajina, nor will we recognise the announced constitution of the quasi-state. We want to continue living in this territory as good neighbours and brothers. We want BiH in a federation of the sovereign republics of Yugoslavia because it's a political fact that four out of six republics are in favour of that solution to the Yugoslav political crisis." Now, were those the views that you had in September of 1991? And apart from you, were those the views of the MBO?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then finally, as you say, the communique ends with a complaint that your brother was called up for military service but not Mr. Kondic. How long -- I'm sorry, did your brother respond to the call-up?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He went to Prijedor. He went to the barracks near the stadium. I don't know what the barracks is called. He was there for three days. On the third day he had to run away from the reserve forces because that was not the army that all of us Bosniaks had sworn for. We swore that we were ready to fight for the JNA and that we were ready to sacrifice our lives if necessary. But this was not for some drunken army. During the day these soldiers would drink, they would watch pornographic films. And when night fell, they would start shooting in the air and they would terrorise the citizens of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So your brother remained three days and then he left?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he left on the third day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you, then, please to look at one more document on the question of mobilisation at this period. Could you look, please, at P859.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Before he does so, Ms. Korner, I have a short question. You were asked to tell the Tribunal who Martic was. I noticed that you mentioned Martic in this document that you've been referred to in the same context as Mount Kozara, the takeover of Mount Kozara TV relay station. Was there a connection between Martic and the incident in Kozara, Mount Kozara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, in my opinion, this was all connected because Martic was a citizen of another state but he moved around our state in Bosnia-Herzegovina, he moved around freely, so that I personally didn't see him issuing orders. I didn't see his men taking the relay station on Kozara. But it was customary for us to say whatever is happening is the responsibility of Martic, Martic is behind this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll hear evidence in relation to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have already.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You've already heard some. And when we get to Bosanska Krupa, Your Honours will hear about Martic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, Exhibit 8 ...?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This again is a document issued some two days after the last that we looked at by the MBO and I think signed by your brother -- or stamped, anyhow. I think there was a signature. The copy is not very good. And it states that the -- in the second paragraph, that "The MBO is opposed to any arming of people which may fall outside the context of orders issued yesterday on the mobilisation of the Territorial Defence and the reserve police force. Any other arming activity and according to our sources such activities are in progress, is only to the detriment of security and peace in the area. Therefore we wish to use this forum and this opportunity to warn those who trust their might to their mace that a mace is a deadly weapon, for he who deals justice with a sword will be slain by a sword. As sworn peace-lovers, we resolutely oppose uncontrolled arming." Now, that -- first of all, the document suggests that there was a call for mobilisation on the 19th of September of 1991. What other arming activities were you referring to in September 1991?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We believed that legal arming was only that of JNA members as they were going to the front and members of the Territorial Defence and the reserve police force. But at that time throughout Bosnian Krajina, particularly in Kljuc, there were helicopters, JNA helicopters, and they would land only in Serb villages. They took out wooden crates, and those of us who served in the army, we knew what was in those wooden crates. So according to the sources that we had and information that we received, they distributed weapons in the Serbian villages, automatic weapons in these Serb villages. This is what this is referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So already by September of 1991 you were receiving reports of arms being delivered to Serb villages; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see a delivery of arms by these helicopters yourself?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally I did not see when a helicopter would land and then weapons unloaded, but I would see the helicopter go round and then land. And for instance, land in Ljubine village. It is unthinkable what an army helicopter -- what work has it got to do in Ljubine village? Why didn't this helicopter land in the village of Zgon or Humici?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Ljubine village is where roughly? I'll ask you to look at a map in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village of Ljubine is located above Zgon. Very near the town of Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would Your Honour forgive me.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a very small village, so it is quite possible that it doesn't appear on some maps.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we just for the moment have a look, please, at the map P1097.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There's no translation of his last statement, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, you had just finished saying, "It's a small village, so it's quite possible it doesn't appear on some maps." Did you say anything else after that? And if you did, what did you say, because the interpreters didn't quite catch it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said "if you bring me the map, I can show you where it is."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. I thank you. Mr. Filipovic, you have the map now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we have it on the ELMO so that Mr. Filipovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. And if you can point on the ELMO. I don't think it is that important to have it marked on the map as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. I think we just want to look at --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that appears to be part of the Muslim area. What ethnicity was most of this village of Ljubine?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serb nationality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the other village which was just Zgon or the other village that you mentioned? What was the ethnicity or the prevailing, if there was?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you said Zgon, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 99.99 per cent Muslim. There was only one Croat family.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What was the distance between one and the other, the two villages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps as the crow flies between 1 and 2 kilometres. But if you walk, it's a little longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Korner, he's in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, thank you. You can put the map away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What effect did the reports of these delivery of arms have on you personally and the Muslims that you knew generally?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think he said there were any reports on delivery of arms. The question states a fact that's not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. I thought --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He didn't testify there were any reports on delivery of arms.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He said he had reports of delivery of arms to -- if Mr. Ackerman goes back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In fact, that's what he said. He said he never saw them himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But he's talking about people telling him. And now she wants know what effect that had on population. He's not talking about public reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's definitely -- now you're qualifying it by public reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: She's talking about facts that don't exist.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I never mentioned the word "public."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. And the question is perfectly legitimate if this is something that he went into and he investigated himself and had feedback from members of his own community or within the party or whatever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Mr. Filipovic, ignore the interruption, please, and tell us --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to make another objection. I'm going to object to her saying ignore the interruption and I'm going to go back to her question -- the evidence that he gave was that he had reports of these deliveries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And her question was: "What effect did the reports of these deliveries of arms have on you personally and the Muslims, that is, that you knew generally." He never said that anybody else got reports but him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But they are still reports. And the question remains perfectly legitimate. I agree with you that Ms. Korner shouldn't tell the witness -- in any case, it should be us who tell him ignore or not ignore and wouldn't say -- wouldn't use the word "ignore." But on the other hand, I think your objection cannot be sustained for a very simple reason that it goes back to square one. He had reports -- now, they were not public reports. You came on a second -- at a second time to tell us that these were public reports. We're not referring to public reports here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I totally agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is information that he received.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I totally agree. But the question was, what effect did they have on the Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, on him is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And also he is a member of a political party.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How did they know. He said he got the reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you never been a member of a political party, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Unfortunately, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So have I. So we all know what we are talking about. So Mr. Filipovic, now please take instructions from me. The question is: Referring to -- look at me, please. Referring to these reports that you referred to before in your testimony, what effect did these reports have on you personally and then on members of -- on Bosniaks that you were familiar with that confided with you their impressions, their reactions, or their concerns with regard to these reports? Let's start with you first. What effect did these reports have on you personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean the reports on the arming through the means of helicopters and such like. Well, you know what the reports were. We lived in a state where we were all citizens of Yugoslavia, Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. And what happened is there were contributions for the JNA out of our income. And suddenly came a period when the JNA is only giving to one ethnic group, to one nation, to one people their weapons. We, the Bosniaks, were completely humiliated, lost any rights. We could see that the war was hanging above our heads. We could see that the war would break out. And in order to try and protect ourselves, to protect our homes, our wives and children, we would have to take out the very last savings to do that, while the Serb people are just given by JNA helicopters literally brought to their door. And I have proof of that. A neighbour of mine by the name of Jovan Blagojevic, who -- he was -- he wasn't bright at all and yet he received weapons. When I asked him why, he said, "Muhis, you just have to. You just have to."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And to your knowledge were other members of the Muslim community in your area, other Bosniaks that you knew, did these reports that were reaching you reach them as well? And if they did, did they confide with you their reaction or concern? Do you know whether you were the only person to receive such information, such reports, or whether there were others that were receiving similar reports?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were others. There were others. There were other citizens, members of Bosniak nationality --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did they share with you your concern?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, with me and with my late brother and with Mr. Egrlic and others, because you could see the helicopter going around above our village. And if a village is easy [as interpreted], to where is he going to go and complain. He's going to come and complain into the town. He's not going to go to the police. He's not going to go to them. He's going to come and complain to Omer Filipovic, Muhamed Filipovic and Egrlic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned this neighbour of yours, Mr. Blagojevic, who received weapons, and you told us that he told you about it. Can you remember what his exact words -- or more or less what his exact words were?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Yes, I can reconstruct accurately the event that happened. My neighbour and a great friend, late Kemo Bender, he came to me and -- and I apologise, Your Honours, that I have to use our words in Bosniak what I have been told. Kemo approached me with this other neighbour, Jovo also being my neighbour -- Kemo told me, "Muhis, fuck the state which gives Jovo a rifle." So I said, "What happened, Kemo?" And he said, "Our Jovo got an automatic rifle." So I said to the two of them, "What happened, Jovo?" And he said, "Muhis, I had to. If I didn't receive a rifle, God know what would have happened to me." So I said to him, "Jovo, make sure you don't use that rifle against Kemo and myself." And he said, "No, I won't." And this very same Jovo is now dead and so is Kemo. Both of them died in Bihac. Kemo was defending it while Jovo was attacking it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And finally on this document - and that may be the appropriate time for a break - in the last paragraph -- well, I'm sorry, there's an invitation in the paragraph before to join -- for the SDS to join talks. And you say, "We want --" I'm sorry, the document says, "We want to talk around a table, not over the barrel of a gun. We advocate peace, not war or arguments," and so on and so forth. And therefore we have arranged inter-party talks of which we expect a lot to take place on Wednesday, 25 September. Do you remember now, did these talks ever take place?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Representatives came of the SDA and MBO, as far as I remember. And the representatives of SDS did not come.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, would that be an appropriate time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We still have a quarter of an hour, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm working on the 2.00. Sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we can proceed, instead of having a break now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I want to move, then, please to -- sorry. Forgive me for one moment -- really to the documents that until the end of September -- I've just lost my list for the moment. Yes. Could we move, please, to -- no, I think that's all. I want to then move with you to documents in December. I want to ask you, please, now Mr. Filipovic about the effect of the mobilisation and the war with Croatia in Kljuc itself between September 1991 and December 1991. What effect did that war have specifically on the events in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, Serb forces as they were leaving for the front towards Croatia and later on to Bosnia, to Kupres, had such influence that people were frightened. People didn't feel like doing anything. The men started sending women and children en masse to Austria, Germany, wherever they worked earlier on in their working years. And the hardest period was when these Serb soldiers were returning from the front. Then they were, I have to say, like maniacs. They would shoot round the town. They would throw hand grenades around the town, from the lorries. God forbid that you were in their way as they were returning on the road. So after every departure and arrival from the front, the people were hurt. They simply did not know what to do. They would say, "What should we do," and then they would come and those who were slightly unstable, they would start crying, saying, "Look what's happening. We're living in a state where some people are haves and the others are have-nots." And the passage of Serb reservists to the front certainly added a great deal to the fact that the people themselves had to organise themselves for the defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in Kljuc, you've told us about your brother's response to the mobilisation call. What sort of proportion of the population -- the Muslim population of Kljuc responded?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to be honest, I don't have the exact data. But if you -- if I give it in percentages, this is not even 1 per cent. A few people responded to the call-up. Perhaps only dozens of people. While there were in Kljuc 18.000 Muslims, so perhaps 10 or 15 only responded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like you now to have a look, please, at document P862. It's a document --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just waiting. I can hear the interpreter flicking over the pages in my earphones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's a document dated the 5th of October, 1991, and it's headed "Staff." It doesn't seem to identify itself in any other way. So can I ask you whether you recognise the names. I think you've already mentioned Veljko Kondic. Who was he?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Veljko Kondic was the director of the post office in Kljuc. He was president of the SDS in Kljuc before he became the director of the post office, I think that he was a lawyer in the Sana factory in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've already told us about Vinko Kondic, your old friend.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vinko Kondic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't worry. Slobodan Jurisic, do you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Slobodan Jurisic, he's a teacher. After, I'm not sure what he did. But I think he's got qualifications as a teacher. I don't know which subject, but he worked at the Secretariat for National Defence. He was a great friend at the time when the League of Communists was in power. He was a friend of Milan Kovacevic. And Milan Kovacevic managed to get him a job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a member of the SDS, do you know?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I presume that he was, because otherwise he wouldn't have remained at such a post, working post had he not been. That's just my assumption.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us very briefly, Lazar Amidzic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lazar Amidzic, he is an economist from Kljuc. I think that the time of war or when the war broke out -- I can't quite tell you what he did, I can't tell you exactly, but I think he was a director of the factory of carpets. For a while he was a bank director. So I'm not quite sure which one of those two posts as a director he was the last.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether he was a member of the SDS or not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I presume, madam, that he was at the time in 1991/1992. Nobody could be at any high post guaranteeing power unless that person was a member of the SDS party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And just one more so that we can deal with the content of this document. Jovo Banjac I think you told us was the president of the municipality; is that right -- of the municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was president of the municipality, but he was a civil engineer and before he became president of the municipality, he was one of the directors at the GP Sana factory. He's dead now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This is just for the transcript. General Talic objects to this document because we don't know who the author of the document is. We don't know where the document was found. We only know that it was given to the OTP by the AID service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I -- that's why I'm going through the document. I should add though that there's a lack of some consistencies in this because some of the documents unsigned and whatever are not -- found from AID are not objected to and others are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but that becomes an argument. It's -- it's a fact but it's predominantly or mainly an argument. So let's leave it for the time being. And for the record, this goes down there is an objection being entered formally by the Defence team for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it is true that some documents that are not signed are not objected to, but this is mostly to do with documents from the radio or from some reports. But this is just what I wanted to say accurately to Mrs. Korner so that she would know what this is about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Next person, Dane Pejic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wasn't going to go any further because we're going to come across these names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I just wanted to establish, if you like, the indicia of reliability.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, I want to ask you about a couple of things in this document. In paragraph 1, Vinko Kondic talks about visiting the Banja Luka and Knin Corps. In October of 1991, were you still on friendly terms with Mr. Kondic -- Mr. Vinko Kondic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was some friendship still, but it wasn't as close as before. When we would stay at each other's houses the night, when we drank in bars. But just in passing we would say hello and how are you, that kind of thing, and then we would just pass by. And already by the end of 1991 our friendship started to break.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us earlier that you were aware that he made visits to Banja Luka because of the drivers or the use of official cars. Did he ever tell you that he had -- himself that he had made a visit to the Banja Luka Corps?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you honestly, he never told me anything personally because a little bit -- he's a little arrogant when he gets to power, Vinko is. So when I told him, "Vinko, you cannot use a municipality vehicle when you're travelling for the party," and then Vinko said, "What are you getting involved in?" And then he then invented this job. And then once we went to Srebrenica precisely because of Vinko. We used the car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. All right. So the answer is the question is he never told you that he was visiting the Banja Luka Corps or anyone else in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. But his duty was to go. Whether -- what he would do there, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It goes on to say that "The conditions in these areas are those of war. You must realise they are trying to spread the war to BH. The Serbs responded well to mobilisation, while the Muslims responded poorly." Then Mr. Jurisic talks about bringing manpower levels up to strength. In the middle of that paragraph, the sentence, "However, everything the army orders, we do. When manpower levels were being brought up to strength, it proved to be 100 per cent Serb soldiers. The Supreme Command made a decision to form the 30th Division." Were you aware of the formation of the 30th Division?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether it was called the 30th Division. I know that when the Croatian authorities forced out the Knin Corps, they made barracks in Laniste. And I know we protested about it. But I don't know whether it was called the 30th Division or some other military term was used, but I know that we called it the Knin Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then finally over the page in the translation, "Information dissemination," Mr. Banjac says that everything is to be censored and it's been left with Mr. Kapetanovic, Veljko Kapetanovic. Is that the person you talked about when we looked at one of the earlier radio station documents?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Veljko Kapetanovic, at that time I believe he was the editor-in-chief of Kljuc Radio.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll break now for the usual 25 minutes, resuming at -- no, at -- quarter of an hour, resuming at 4.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I'm sorry, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want for a moment, please, Mr. Filipovic, to stick to the topic of the arming that you have been talking about of Serbs and then look at the Muslim reaction in terms of arms and organisations. Could you for a moment, please, have a look at document which is numbered P887.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's objected to, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we've contested this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, first of all, can you --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could Madam Fauveau just remind me on what grounds this one is objected to, because it's signed and sealed apparently.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It has no number and it has no date. And it was obtained by -- through the intermediary of the AID agency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, first of all, Mr. Filipovic, can you tell us, do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vinko Kondic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. What's the stamp on it? Do you recognise that stamp?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a stamp of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what sort -- in your experience as a member of the assembly, what sort of documents would this stamp be placed on?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This stamp would be placed on important documents brought in to the Ministry of Defence or to the Ministry of the Interior. On all documents in Bosnia, there would be a stamp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As is pointed out, this document is undated, and it's a list of names. I don't want you to go through every name, but can you tell us, do you recognise any of the names?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just tell us which ones.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just cast a glance at it. Kuburic Boro, Kuburic Radenko, Micanovic Stojan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what number?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 3, number 4, number 6, number 11, 12, 13, number 16.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. It will do. These people, what nationality were they?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were Serbs. I think that this is a list of people armed by the local commune and the Ministry of the Interior, that is to say, the police provided them with weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And I think I want you to look at one other document, please. Yes. Could you look at, please, P891.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, this is objected to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this appears to be a diary of some sort or a diary page. It's blank and we don't know the date, but I would actually imagine it would be May of 1992 if it's anything. That's just the diary. It says: "Distribution of weapons from depot. Take out all weapons and by the given deadline distribute to individuals on the list adopted at the latest session of the Peci local commune." What sort of a place was Peci? In other words -- first of all, where was Peci?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The local commune of Peci is on the road between Kljuc and Sanski Most. It's between the village of Kamicak and the village of Krasulje. Kamicak is a Muslim village and Krasulje, a Muslim village too, whereas Peci is a village which is 100 per cent Serb and the local commune had its headquarters there. Slobodan, a salesman in Zadar, he was active in the local commune.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is the person who probably compiled this report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what makes you say that? Oh, because -- I can see, because it's signed, "Slobodan." I'm sorry. He was a salesman.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what kind of a salesman?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, before the rise of nationalism, people thought he was a good salesman. And in Bosnia, as opposed to in the West, the shops are small, so one salesman worked in a shop in one village and sold food, and he worked in a mixed goods shop which provided for the needs of the village. They provided food, petroleum, some textiles, et cetera. That was a mixed goods shop, which was in the community home in Peci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we just look at the other entries briefly. This record was made and approved by the president of the Peci local commune, the proposal of the Serbian Democratic community of the Kljuc municipality and approval was also granted by the Assembly of the Republican Democratic SDS with its seat at Pale. And then under the page for Saturday, May: "In forthcoming days a certain quantity of packages for the Serbian people should be expected and the packages immediately distributed." And then finally under that: "List of personnel for destruction and the destruction of their material property. This list includes all persons who are not members of the Serbian people, principally the Muslim population." All right. You can put that document away. Thank you very much. Before I come to a document for December 1991, as a result of the events that you have described, what actions did the MBO decide to take?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The MBO, cooperating with the SDA, attempted to prepare the people as much as possible for the situation that was going to develop in Kljuc. These activities of ours were such that we would visit inhabited places and we would speak to the people there. But we could only do this through speaking to people. It wasn't possible to have public gatherings because we would immediately be considered as Muslim fundamentalists and they would consider us to be involved in an uprising. But some of us went into a village and with some prominent people from the village we would hold conversations, we would then split up, have some coffee. And then the people who remained in the village, they would relay this information to the people. And in this document you can see what I have mentioned, what I mentioned earlier on. These were packets that were brought in by helicopter. And we had to warn the people about this because we had information, and this relates to what you have just asked me about, madam, because as I said, Bosnia was mixed. There were people who had failed. They were losers who would do anything for a cognac. They'd sit down, have a drunk, and everything would be found out. So that's how we found out things too. That's how we obtained information. There were such people, such losers in addition to the regular people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We're going to see reference in later documents to a patriotic league. Who formed that patriotic league?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to Kljuc or ...?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosnia-Herzegovina? Well, several of us who were in charge of the MBO and SDA parties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the purpose of that patriotic league being what?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Kljuc it was just to prepare the people for what was going to happen, because from the time that war broke out in Croatia onwards, we were 100 per cent convinced that Moljevic's plan to form a greater Serbia was being implemented, and we knew on the basis of the massing of Serbian forces, we knew where they were being deployed. We knew what would happen. And we knew that war would break out in our town of Kljuc too. It was just a matter of days. So we attempted to prepare the people for what was going to happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Roughly in Kljuc, leaving aside Bosnia-Herzegovina, how many Muslims or non-Serbs joined the patriotic league?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, when the war broke out in Croatia in the first wave a small number because the people were suspicious. They would approach us with suspicion. So perhaps in the year of 1991 about 50 people. But then as the war escalated in Croatia, in my opinion, because we didn't have any records, we were -- we existed on a legal basis in Kljuc at the time. If something would be agreed on a meeting, we would write this down in code and then we would destroy it later on. So I'd say about 100, 150 people. This is just an estimate of mine. That differed from the Territorial Defence, that's the difference between the patriotic league and the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just one very minor interruption, just to make it clear. You did mention a plan to form a greater Serbia. And the transcript says here Moljevic. Did you say "Moljevic" or "Milosevic"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Moljevic. Moljevic. That was a Serbian politician from the nineteenth century.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, from out of that patriotic league, did you yourselves then form a Crisis Staff? Again, we'll see reference in some documents later to that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was on that Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were seven or eight people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you one of the people?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your brother?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Asim Egrlic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A gentleman named Amir Avdic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think others -- and I'm not going to bother to go through them. No doubt you'll be asked about them if they're thought to be relevant. Who was head of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Roughly at what stage did you form this Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date, but I think it was in the second half of 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did you feel it necessary to have a Crisis Staff within that patriotic league?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, madam, because it was easier for five or six people to have a meeting than 50 people. And if there was something for us to carry out, it was easier for the five of us to meet and to agree on something -- it was easier to do that than to try and gather 50 people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you actually call yourselves a Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the sake of form, yes, we called ourselves such. Because in the Bosnian language there's a headquarters for everything. So if we're harvesting, we say "the harvesting headquarters," et cetera. So all those people who were in charge of something, who have positions of responsibility, they have a headquarters. If there's some sort of a crisis, for example, when there was an earthquake, you would select a few people and then one would say they're in charge of the Crisis Staff. So this word is a word which is part of our vocabulary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, other than forming this Crisis Staff, you told us that you were aware that the Serbs from 1991 onwards, from the war in Croatia had been providing -- had been given arms. Did you make any attempts to obtain arms that could be distributed to the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We tried to and in various ways. The only legal means which we found -- well, we managed to -- in the local Territorial Defence which had been mobilised by the Serbs at the time, we managed to get Muslims to be included from certain areas, but they had to remain within the territory of the municipality of Kljuc. I don't know how long they were there, but for a certain period of time they responded to the mobilisation and they were part of the Territorial Defence. They were issued weapons, but when returning home they had to return the weapons. When they went home, they had to return their weapons to the units. This was not the case for certain Serbs who would take their weapons with them. But we also considered this to be progress, because when people went on patrol, there were Muslims who were on guard with Serbs in villages, and all of our weapons -- well, we armed ourselves by having people buy their own weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to leave aside the events of 1992 for a moment and just concentrate on 1991. By the -- December of 1991 what sort of arms had you acquired? You've told that you were having people buy weapons.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had a pistol, 7.65 millimetre calibre. The general is over there. He knows what kind of a pistol that is. I bought it with my own money. I paid 1.100 marks for it and I had a permit for this. 80 per cent of the population bought weapons. When Serbian soldiers came back from the front in Kupres, they would sell weapons. And only later I personally -- only when I was arrested in Manjaca in Stara Gradiska I realised that this is something that -- a trap that had been laid for us by the Serbs, because for me as a man it was illogical. If I've bought a weapon from a Serb, how can there be someone in Manjaca who knows from whom I bought this weapon? So I consider this to be something that was arranged with the leaders of the SDS. There was an agreement that the Muslims should be armed or if they bought weapons such as Zoljas, heavier weapons, well, for example you'd get a Zolja without a part, with some sort of deficiency, and the Zolja would not be functional but you would pay a lot of money for it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just pause there for a moment, please. You said that -- that a trap had been laid for you by the Serbs, and you discovered this when you were in Manjaca and Stara Gradiska. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I would tell Your Honours that it is not logical that if I am smuggling, I'm doing some sort of smuggling, I'm involved in some kind of criminal activity, how can a superior know that I had sold to somebody such and such a rifle, and it is unthinkable, because when I was serving in the JNA the weapons were not supposed to be taken out of the army, so it is unthinkable that it is possible for weapons just to be carried just like that. And then this person who came to be interrogated later on, they had exactly the number, the serial number of the rifle and all the details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when people like yourself were being interrogated in one of these camps, you're saying that the Serbs would put to them that they -- that you had a particular gun with a particular serial number. So they knew about it.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Specifically speaking, they knew about my case. They took the weapon away from me. I had a legally owned gun, a handgun, a pistol, because MUP gave me a permit. But people who bought guns from the Serbs, this was illegally acquired weapons. But the Serbs knew about that as well. In a position to what I had as weapons or for instance, if someone in Kljuc was a hunter, it was all legal. They had a permit. It was all registered. So we have to make a separation. We have legally owned weapons, permits issued by MUP, handguns or hunting rifles. So they could have these numbers. But in my view, it was not possible to have the numbers of this other illegally acquired weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, two other matters just before the end of 1991. First, why did you and other Muslims that you knew feel it necessary to acquire weapons?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how I could answer this. I could only tell you by asking you a question. What would you do if you were watching that someone was planning to do harm to your child or to your husband? In some way you would have to defend yourself. It was just the question of day, when we would be eliminated. And we couldn't get any help from anyone. What could we do? Die honourably, or be lambs to the slaughter?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll take it that was a rhetorical question. Second -- again can we just concentrate. December of 1991, roughly how many arms had been acquired that you knew about by the end of December 1991? And by "you," -- I'm sorry, how many arms you had acquired, I mean the Muslims in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my approximate estimate, this would include the weapons that people had as hunting weapons and the weapons like the one I had, a handgun, and also illegally acquired from the Serbs as they were coming from the front.
