I didn't count it. I would estimate it as between five and seven hundred pieces of weapons. I believe that's what we had, except that the hardest part was of course the ammunition. If we had a rifle or a pistol, we would only have 20, 30 bullets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you acquiring any weaponry -- and by "you," I mean the organisation, the Crisis Staff -- from outside Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with great difficulty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how much were you getting from sources outside Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall this. I only remember that there was a small delivery just some Heckler guns, automatic guns from Croatia. That's what I remember that we received. But I cannot tell you how many of them there were. This is a 9 millimetre calibre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The weaponry that you owned outside hunting rifles and pistols, what sort of quality of weaponry was it? Was it modern weaponry or older weaponry?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you honestly, when I said "five to seven hundred pieces of weapons," a large number of them were old-fashioned handguns. These were Kuburas [phoen]. These were very old-fashioned handguns. I don't know whether Your Honours know what this is. These were handguns from the Middle Ages. They would be kept by people -- if somebody broke into the house, they would be able to defend themselves. Now, defending oneself with these old fashioned handguns from tanks and multiple rocket launchers, that is not at all appropriate. And for the most part the weapons we had were old fashioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll come back to that when we look at some of the documents later. But could you now please look at the document numbered P865.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, this is objected to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's headed -- I think if you have the original rather than the -- yes, they're copied together actually -- headed "Minutes of the sixth meeting of the executive committee of the SDS municipal board in Kljuc held on the 23rd of December, 1991." And we then see the agenda. And I want to do the same thing I did with the last document, and that's go through the people who are mentioned here. Under agenda item 1, apparently Veljko Kondic informed the meeting of the instructions for the organisation and activities of the Serbian people in BH. "All organs will be required to act in accordance with those instructions. Whoever is not ready to fulfil his duties should say so immediately and it will not be held against him." And you've already told us who he was. Then the next gentleman who's mentioned Vlado Uncanin, who was he?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vlado Uncanin, he was a member of the top leadership of the SDS in Kljuc SDS. He worked in the electricity supply factory in Kljuc and in the -- and in Sanica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then the next person, I think a lady, Jovanka Cvijic, do you know who she was?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jovanka Cvijic. At the time when she needed it, she was Tito's youth club member. He worked in the Sipad work community. I'm not quite sure which department, but I know that she worked at the Sipad work community.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know whether or not she was a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since she attended this meeting, I believe she was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then next somebody called Brane Vojvodic, who says he can accept all Karadzic proposals without seeing them. Do you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness approach the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, could you lean forward, yes, for the microphone. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was Brane Vojnovic, not Vojvodic. And he's a citizen of Sanica. He worked at the factory in Sanica. I believe that he was a warehouse keeper. He declared himself a Vojvoda at the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And then Mr. Kondic goes on to say that all -- "That means that all suggestions and tasks from the instructions are accepted in their entirety." And it sets out the composition of the Crisis Staff. And then we see under item 6 "Deputy in the assembly, vice-president of the executive committee of the municipal assembly, Dragan Smiljanic." Do you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragan Smiljanic was not a deputy at the assembly. He's a doctor, a physician in Kljuc. Dragan Smiljanic at the time -- when we were children, his nickname was Grsa. He used his participation in the SDS and managed to get hold of a permit to build a house where he wasn't supposed to build one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then Ljuban Bajic, who I think we're going to see on the video. Who was he?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ljuban Bajic, a teacher. At the time before the war he was a Communist and he worked for the League of Communists. He managed to get a qualification of a teacher working part time. My brother helped him. By the time of the aggression, as far as I believe, he was a SDS spokesperson.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then Vinko Kondic went on to say that "We have to implement the federal and not Bosnian laws because the Bosnian laws are passed by outvoting the Serbs." "Velko Kondic, will be responsible for cooperation with the SDA. Tihomir Dakic will be responsible for the municipal assembly reserves." Who was Mr. Dakic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tihomir Dakic was a vice-president of the executive committee. He was a member of the Crisis Staff of the SDS. And according to the information that I had, sometime in 1993 or 1994, as far as I know he parted ways with these ideas. He wasn't happy. Otherwise, he's an economist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We've dealt with Mr. Jurisic. Bosko Lukic, who we see written there, who was he?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosko Lukic, he was a teacher of people's defence. I believe he was the commander of Territorial Defence. I don't know what it's called, but in any case he worked at the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And over the page for us. But we see that Mr. Kalabic was there, who we've identified as the SDS member of the regional --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kalabic is a deputy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then Milan Jovicic. It says: "I think that the Assembly of the Serbian Municipality of Kljuc should be proclaimed at the assembly session. I ask that this meeting be informed about the second stage." First of all, who was Mr. Jovicic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan Jovicic is a mechanical engineer. I believe that he was the director of the sewing mill [as interpreted] in Kljuc. He was, unless I'm very much mistaken, he was a deputy at the Kljuc Municipal Assembly. And we knew about his viewpoints, that he was talking about in the session. From our own channels, we knew that the Serbs were preparing to declare a Serbian Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was going to ask you that, because we're going to see what you, the Muslims, did. When did you first become aware that the SDS were proposing to, as it were -- as you said, declare a Serbian Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew that by the end of 1991. And we were -- that hit us in the head when -- I believe that it was in the last ten days in December 1991, when 25 buses of Croats were forced out of Slunj, and they were stopped by the Serb police. They were mistreated. They were beaten. And then we knew for sure that this had to happen, that this was going to happen very soon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I think we can deal with the next item on the agenda fairly quickly. This was talking about the formation of companies and the like. And then if we come down, please, to apparently what somebody called Jovan Kevac said. He said: "If war starts in BH, we should pull our people back from the war zones into this area. We have to take care only of the Serbian population. I advise the Crisis Staff that we should arm our people. The Crisis Staff should do more to keep the Serbian people informed." Who was Mr. Kevac? Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jovan Kevac was the commander of the Territorial Defence before Bosko Lukic. I don't know what he did exactly. He was some kind of a clerk. But he was Captain First Class at the JNA reserves. And as this happens, Serbs had to be leaders or managers, and he was posted as the main administrator for people's defence and self-protection at the Sumarska or forestry department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just to complete this document finally, Ljuban Bajic says all of us are right. "Can we find a compromise so that we would have our own option if it comes to war." And Bosko Bajic -- I can't remember whether I asked you about him. I don't think I did. Who was Bosko Bajic, if you knew him?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for Bosko Bajic, I couldn't tell you 100 per cent who he is. Very vaguely. I am trying to remember. There were several Bajics, but I actually don't wish to tell you and then make a confusion as far as people are concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, he seems to have something to do with the Territorial Defence because he says that "Everything having to do with the Territorial Defence has to be finished by the 10th of January, 1992. Issue a decision to dismiss the current Territorial Defence commander." Can we pause there for a moment. In December 1991, who was -- what nationality was the commander of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. As far as I know, the commander was Bosko Lukic as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And then finally, D, "Since 400 people have left for the war zones, we have the right to demand weapons and I advise that the president schedules a meeting with Talic and to ask for weapons and to make that the accepted conclusion of the executive committee." All right. That document, I think, brings us to the end of December 1991. You've told us that you were -- you, the Muslims, were aware of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, in the B/C/S version of this document, the last page, bottom of the page, left corner, there seems to be what appears to be a signature. Perhaps ask the witness whether he's familiar with that signature, whether he recognises that signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, you've heard the question. Do you recognise either the writing or the signature?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recognise it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recognise it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Bosko Lukic, what ethnicity was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's move then, please, to January -- no, I'm sorry, before we do that, can I ask you this: As a result of what you say you knew, that they were going to set a Serbian -- set up a Serbian Kljuc, did you and the MBO and/or the SDA take any decision as to what you were going to do?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We decided that we would go before them, that we would do that before they did. So we were the only town in Bosnia-Herzegovina in opposition to the Serbs who gave a prefix of "Serb" to everything they were going to declare or proclaim as Serbian Kljuc, while we proclaimed or declared Bosnian Kljuc because we lived in Bosnia, and there's no way that you can say "Serbian Kljuc" in Bosnia or Hungarian or Dutch, because it could only be Bosnian. We did not want to call it Muslim Kljuc but we wanted to call it Bosnian Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can we then look please next at document P869.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we've already -- I'm sorry, Your Honour, I seem to have ticked that on my list. We may already have looked at that with the witness. Maybe not. Let's just check it. Could the witness have it. Sorry. My fault.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This on the 16th of January allegedly confirms that the -- Kljuc will join -- I'm sorry, let's be a bit more careful -- that representatives from the Kljuc Municipal Assembly to the Assembly of Banja Luka regional community are confirmed as legally and legitimately elected representatives and that the president of the Kljuc Municipal Assembly is hereby authorised to sign again the adequate documents on the membership of the Kljuc municipality in the Autonomous Region, and it will enter into force on the day of its adoption. Were you -- was this matter debated in the assembly in January of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In December 1991 we left the assembly, and this decision was issued without the presence of Muslim deputies. At that time Muslim and later on Bosniak ethnicity. It was in December 1991 that we left the assembly, and to our call to leave the assembly other opposition deputies also left the assembly who were of Muslim ethnicity. So this decision was passed without the presence of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We can see in its preamble it talks about -- or the document states that "The Kljuc Municipal Assembly at its 10th session held on the 26th of December, 1991 adopted the following." Had you left before that date, or was it on that date, the 26th of December, that you left?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was on the 26th of December. Don't take this for certain, but I think that was the date that we left, because I know it was towards the end of December, but I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the reason that you and the other opposition parties left the assembly?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was the main obstacle. The SDS wanted to put on the agenda accession to the Autonomous Region of Bosnian Krajina, and we didn't want to do this, and we were just a screen for them, to enable them to pass through a law for which they required two-thirds majority. And at that point we said that this item of ours should be after this one and that we would be present. They kept us there until this item appeared on the agenda. Once this item appeared, my late brother rose up. He called the president and the engineer Banjac and he said, "Engineer, we haven't agreed on this." He said, "So what are you going to do then, teacher?" And that's when he left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, can you turn, please, to the -- or can you be given, please, the next document, 870. It's dated the 30th of January. And again, it's a Radio Kljuc broadcast, headed "Municipality of Bosanski Kljuc." And it says, "At yesterday's session of the SDA and the MBO deputies' club, the formation of a new municipality of Bosanski Kljuc was proclaimed which does not accept the unlawful and unconstitutional decisions of the municipal assembly concerning the inclusion of this municipality into the Autonomous Region of the Bosnian Krajina." And it says that "This is the first part of the official statement handed out to journalists at today's press conference by Omer Filipovic, who was elected the first president of this municipality and deputy president of the Kljuc Municipal Assembly." And Filipovic said "The interim assembly of the Bosanski Kljuc municipality had also adopted several decisions: To call a referendum ... And to accept the existing Kljuc municipality as long as it respects the constitution and the laws of Bosnia and Herzegovina," and so on and so forth. And over the page in English it says this: "The administrative organs of the Kljuc Municipal Assembly are required to respect the laws of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and to pay tax and contributions into the budget and the funds of the Republic rather than those of the Autonomous Region of the Bosnian Krajina." Now, on that, what had been happening about the payment of taxes and contributions to the Bosnian budget?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, as far as taxes and contributions are concerned, well, it is on this basis that the state can function. And when the SDS took over all power, it cut the transfer of payments and in the so-called Autonomous Region Bosnian Krajina taxes and contributions were redirected to Banja Luka instead of going to Sarajevo. And in our opinion, it was illogical for us to have a state and for our taxes and contributions not to go to the centre of the state but to Banja Luka. And it's from that town that they would make payments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then finally the document ends by saying: "It is also true that this is the first Muslim municipality in Bosnia and Herzegovina, but its fate depends on the move of the partner, the SDS, because if there is no regionalisation on an ethnic basis, then there will be no municipality of Bosanski Kljuc either." Can you just explain what was meant by that.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that meant that if the SDS stops carrying out its actions and considers that there is no Serbian Kljuc in Kljuc, then we too would declare that there was no such thing as a Bosnian Kljuc, that there was only one Kljuc. And we would immediately join the structures of the municipal assembly in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, when the Assembly of Bosanski Kljuc was established in January of 1992, where did it meet?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It met in the centre, the social centre in Pudin Han. Those are the suburbs of Velagici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you move, please, to -- can we look at P874. Now, this is apparently an announcement dated the 3rd of February of 1992. And it says: "From the beginning of the war to today, the Serbian armed forces conducting fast and energetic operations have completely broken up the Muslim combat formations on the territory of our municipality. Only small and isolated groups of the most hardened extremists remain, although they are disoriented. Unfortunately, they have not stopped provoking the defence forces of the Kljuc municipality, thereby inflicting the greatest damage on themselves and their own people. And therefore, we again call on the Muslim people to hand over their remaining weapons and to help capture and hand over these lunatics." Now, this is February 1992, and it's not known -- well, perhaps you can help. Do you recall any sort of announcement like this?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is just one of the games that the SDS played. And I personally think that this is one of the many lies, because in February 1992 there were no conflicts, no armed conflicts in Kljuc. And I can claim this for sure. There were verbal disputes, et cetera, through announcements over the radio, but in February 1992 there was no armed conflict because -- there was no shooting in Kljuc until the 25th of May, 1992. And that's three months. There are three months between these dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question was: Do you recall any sort of an announcement like this? And I don't think it's been answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He hasn't answered the question, yes. Indirectly he has, giving us the impression that this was only one of several. But do you recall this particular announcement? Do you recall having heard or come across this particular announcement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were announcements, as many as you like. But on the 3rd of February, 1992 there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I would object to this document unless there can be some showing that it -- that it actually was an announcement rather than just a piece of paper. You know, announced how? To whom? By whom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You are --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It has no force if it never got out of somebody's file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll come to that later on, Mr. Ackerman. I can tell you that if that is of concern to you, it is of concern to us. Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We also object to this document, and I have informed Mrs. Korner of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In a letter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I'll make a point when I reach documents which I know are objected to by Madam Fauveau of indicating that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So Mr. Filipovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have five minutes. So that's --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Because I was going to move to the next document, Your Honour. Which may -- it will be a larger topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Shall we stop now?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll have a break, resuming at -- 15 minutes from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Could you have a look, please, at document P875. This document, Mr. Filipovic, is a report emanating from the 5th Corps in Banja Luka, as it then was, dated the 11th of February, 1992. And I want you to have a look, please, at paragraph number 4, entitled "Situation in the territory." And could you at the same time, please, be given the map that was exhibited as P1079. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if that could go up on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It states this: "In the sector of Laniste on the Kljuc-Bosanski Petrovac road the inhabitants of the villages of Pudin Han, Velagici, Hadzici, Castovici --"

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Castovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Castovici, yes. "Hadzici are holding rallies and barricades and demonstrations may be expected. The reason for the rallies is they expect the arrival of JNA units." If we look, first of all, at the map, we can see Laniste, Pudin Han, Velagici, Hadzici is not marked -- oh, it is, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I think the only one that's not marked is the one I can't pronounce. Castovici, whereabouts is that place?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village of Castovici is above the village of Hadzici. It's a very small village inhabited by Muslims. So -- so that it doesn't appear on these kind of maps. It should appear on a military map, ratio 1 to 25.000. On such a map it would be possible to see the village of Castovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you know anything about rallies and demonstrations taking place in February having something to do with the arrival of JNA?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And on several occasions I have pointed out that the people were unhappy about the transfer of the units of the Knin Corps from Croatia to Bosnia-Herzegovina. And in the area of Laniste, where there is a forestry company, a forestry workshop, on the basis of the decision of those in power at the time, of the authorities in the so-called autonomous region of Bosnian Krajina, it was necessary to construct a barracks there. And this was in fact done. So a forestry area was turned into a barracks for the Knin Corps. And as proof, anyone who likes could go to Kljuc. The remains of the building are still there. It was built in a very short period of time. It's a building on three floors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. What I really was asking about was why didn't the inhabitants in this particular area want the Knin Corps to be posted there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because the people were expecting what was to happen. Citizens of Muslim and Croat nationality knew that those soldiers who had been transferred from Croatia, they knew that they only bore the false name of the JNA. In fact, it was the Serbian army and the people were unhappy because it wasn't an army protecting all the peoples. They were only protecting one people and people weren't happy about this. And in the Laniste area, that is the only place where it is possible to obstruct the arrival of the corps from the direction of Knin without putting civilians at risk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether those demonstrations actually took place?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't call them demonstrations. These were small gatherings, small gatherings of people. There were such gatherings, but as usual they lied to the people. Nothing was to come of that. Jovo Banjac, the notorious Jovo Banjac came out. And our people are easily misled. And he said that nothing is going to happen, and the people disbursed. And overnight an order was issued to the Sana company, an order according to which the building was to be constructed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You can leave that document now. And can we go, please, to Exhibit P877.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document apparently - and it's not easy to see - but it's the SDS Kljuc municipal committee that also relates back to the Serbian Democratic -- the SDS executive committee in Sarajevo, apparently. And it's to do apparently with the appointment of judges and legal positions in Kljuc. And if you go to the paragraph that begins "During the division of power in the municipality, the SDA was allotted the position of president of the court and the judge of Muslim nationality is currently holding this position. In addition to the president of the court, another judge of the Muslim nationality is currently working at the court and the appointment of additional two judges of Muslim nationality to this important state organ would be completely - it must be - would be to completely disrupt the ethical equality. This would be particularly unacceptable in the area where the Serbs are in a majority and where the SDS won more than 52 per cent of voices and the SDA 33 per cent." And then it goes on to deal with -- There was a candidate of Muslim nationality, Nihad Filipovic. Now, first of all, is that any relation of yours?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nihad Filipovic. Yes, we're brothers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was your brother.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're the children of two brothers -- the children of two brothers. My father and his father are brothers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. That makes it clear. As far as the rationale -- in the end they end up -- this is obviously being submitted to Sarajevo. They end up recommending that a Serb judge, Rajko Dakic, be appointed. Was this something that was -- I'm sorry; I'll rephrase that question. You've told us earlier that there had to be allocation between the different nationalities of various positions. Was this in fact consistent with the normal allocation, or was this unusual?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, this is unusual with regard to the previous arrangement, because after the first multi-party elections, the president of the court, this position, belonged to deputies of the SDA and the MBO. And this post was occupied by Dzemo Botonic [phoen] -- the judge Dzemo Botonic. So if in a multinational environment such a court was to survive, then it would be necessary for someone to be elected as president from the Muslim people. Or if there were some sort of reshuffling, they could have given us one position and we could have given them a different position. We could have exchanged positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, that document leads me on to what I want to ask you in respect of jobs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. You can leave the document now -- or give it back to the usher. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By February/March of -- by February of 1992, there was this split. There were two assemblies: One the Bosanski Kljuc and one the Kljuc original assembly. Was there any movement then, this period, to dismiss non-Serbs from their employment?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. There were no dismissals in February. But there were other incidents, maltreatment, lack of -- unemployment. So in my example, in the case of the job that I carried out, I only had members of Muslim nationality in my party. No Serb wanted to come to me in that period. My clients were never Serbs. No one came to me as a Serb surveyor to carry out some sort of work. They all asked for colleagues of Serbian nationality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before this period, so before, let's say, mid-1991, would you be employed by persons of all nationality or just by persons of Muslim nationality?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's my fault. It was a dual question. Do you mean yes you would have been employed by persons of all nationalities?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, by both.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can we move, please, then to the next document very briefly, just to look at one thing in connection with the matters you've spoken of. It's P878.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again, I should tell Your Honour I think this is objected to. It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we've objected to it. All these reports are objected to because they have no signature and we don't know who the author is, and we don't know if they correctly reflect the contents of these sessions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's quite right. They don't have a signature. But in the sense that we can't identify who the signature's is. But may I say that for Madam Fauveau's benefit, I'm just indicating as we go through the ones that are objected to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you both.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under agenda item 1 -- and this relates back to something you've told us about -- B, the Assembly of the -- I think that must be Autonomous Region of Banja Luka was held where there were opinions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope it is. And it's not something else, because that would open other doors.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I think it must be -- I don't know what -- anyhow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it was understood that -- I'm sorry, "Where there were opinions that the Republic of Bosnian Krajina should be formed, but it was understood that this was not the time for that." And "They then talked about the conference regarding BH and cannonisation. All revenues would belong to the region. The national bank would be based in Banja Luka ... And certain services will be dislocated from Sarajevo. He spoke about the unfavourable structure of those employed in the SDK in Kljuc and the decision was made that all public funds would be held in Banja Luka." This was in March of 1992. Did you become aware that this was the decision that had been made?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was when they severed the transfer of payments to Sarajevo. That's when that happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That severance of payments to Sarajevo, what effect did that have on people?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, whoever received salaries from Sarajevo was not able to receive that salary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I said there was only one item. If we then, look, under agenda item 3, which was "Information about defence preparations." There was a briefing by Mr. Veljko Kondic and Mr. Banjac suggests that "All Territorial Defence weapons should be taken to Kula." Where was that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kula is on the main road between Kljuc and Mrkonjic Grad. It's in the immediate vicinity of the tourist site Balkana. When you go from the direction of Kljuc to Mrkonjic, it's on the left-hand side. It's a JNA building. That's where they had barracks and they had some sort of underground structures, those sort of things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You can put that document away. Can we move, then, to the next document, P880. Again, Your Honour, objected to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, minutes of a meeting of the SDS in Kljuc held on the 12th of March. And the discussion, as we can see, really centres around weapons and arming. At the bottom of the page, Mr. Kondic -- Mr. Veljko Kondic says that "We will undertake to get additional weapons." Around this period of March 1992, did you become aware of these decisions - obviously not the documents themselves - but that there was a decision being taken to build up weaponry and arms generally?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already answered that question. Throughout the period of time when there were helicopters flying, and that was during March and February -- we're not fools. We knew that there was something happening, some sort of decisions were being implemented. The pilot of the helicopter can't fly without being ordered to do so. He can't use up fuel without having received the order. Someone must have ordered him to fly to a certain destination and to unload cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You told us -- sorry -- this was happening in 1991. We're now in March of 1992. Was there any obvious signs, or did you require any information that there was more of a build-up going on?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, obviously there is some sort of a misunderstanding, madam. I said from 1991 and right up until the time when the aggression started there were helicopters flying over it. It wasn't just in 1991. It was in the year 1992 as well. If we received any kind of information, we'd get it from drunken soldier of some kind. And after returning from the battlefield, he'd provide us with this information. That was the only source of information. If we had a drunken soldier who provided us with such information, then we'd link up the information provided by two or three people and discover what was happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Yes. Thank you. All right. Can we now look, please, at Exhibit 882, P882. This is a report, again coming from the -- in fact, it comes from the 1st Krajina Corps collection, but it's a report on the formation of the 13th Partisan Brigade and addressed to the command of the 30th Partisan Division, signed by Lieutenant Colonel Samardzija. It describes under item 2 "The command of the 13th Partisan Brigade has the following information about non-establishment units of the 13th Partisan Brigade and the TO in Kljuc, 100 armed men, SDS, and then the type of weapons." And then over the page, please, under paragraph 3, there's this paragraph: "It is estimated that there are several paramilitary formations/units in the area of responsibility, including in Kljuc municipality, Kljuc itself, two companies; in Sanica, one battalion; Krasulje, two companies being formed." And if we skip out Mrkonjic Grad and Sipovo. "The paramilitary units formed in the municipalities of Kljuc and Sipovo are made up of Muslims ...." Now, at this stage in March of 1992, had there been formed in Kljuc itself - and I imagine it means Kljuc town - two companies made up of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not true. That's not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any sort -- had you or anyone else organised any sort of actual military companies within Kljuc town itself by March of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We tried to organise ourselves. But Your Honours, it says here that Kljuc had two companies, Sanica, one battalion and Krasulje two companies that are being formed. If we had had this many people that are under arms, the SDS would not have forced us out of Kljuc in 1992. We would have stayed in Kljuc. We would have defended our homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, just tell Their Honours -- they may already know, but how many men would two companies be, roughly?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to my estimate, when I was serving in the military, one company is about 150 people. A battalion is 500-plus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Can we look, then, briefly please at the next document in the bundle, which is P606.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This was, Madam Fauveau, ex-Exhibit P883.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It had already been exhibited, so we had to change the number. It's behind divider 45, for the purposes of the usher. All right. I don't want to -- because there's only one line. In fact, I can deal with it without asking the witness to look at the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By March of 1992 in Kljuc had there been any incidents of violence in the town itself?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was. As far as I can recall, there were murders. But I cannot now tell you whether that was in March, late March, or whether it was early April. But in the municipality of Kljuc, there were two murders that took place where drunken reservists on their way back from the front, they killed two young men. One young man was killed in Kljuc near the bus station, and the second young man was killed in Sanica. But I cannot tell you whether that was March or April, but I know that this was during that time period. And it is known who killed them, but that was the end of story.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. This -- can we just look very briefly. Now you've been given this report which is dated the 28th of March from the 5th Corps that. It states that on the 27th of March, 1992 a hand grenade was thrown in front of the Galleria cafe in Kljuc and it exploded. First of all, do you remember such an incident? If not, say so.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that a hand grenade was thrown. As I spoke earlier, I'm not quite sure whether this is 27th of March or not. It was near that time when the young man Dervisevic was killed that was in the immediate vicinity of Galleria.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know who owned the Galleria Cafe?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The coffee bar, Galleria, belongs to a Serb who is currently living in Kljuc. I can't remember his name, but the coffee bar is still there. A Muslim is managing it while the owner gets the rent. I cannot recall his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't worry. Thank you. Yes. Thank you. You can hand that document back to the usher.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think we need bother -- all right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to now try and get the picture, please, before the Court of the situation in the run-up to May the 27th. When did there first start to be barricades and the like being set up?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean the barricades?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the first time that the Muslims decided to set up barricades?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the 25th of May, after the 25th of May, when the village of Crljeni - we don't have any evidence whether it was attacked or whether the people came to do the reconnaissance of the field - but at that time a group of people was captured, a group of soldiers was captured, five to ten of them -- I don't know exactly how many of them there were. They were captured. Their documents were showing that they were from Serbia. And they were captured in Crljeni on the 25th of May. From that day onwards, we considered ourselves under attack. And the most critical period started in Kljuc on the 7th of May, when the Serbs took over the police officially, because it was on the 7th of May that they took over the police. They asked the policemen who were of Muslim or Croat ethnicity to sign allegiance. When these men refused, these policemen were sacked, and they had to leave the public security station. And on the 7th of May, they put out a Serb flag on the police station and the municipality. This is when the critical period started, the crisis period started in the Kljuc municipality. There were no conflicts, but from the 7th of May onwards it started to become tense. I was personally present when they put the flag out on the police station, because this is -- I passed by there on my way back from work, and I remember very well Mrs. Andja Pejic told me, "Look how beautiful it is, the Serbian flag."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, before the 7th of May, at any stage had you or any of your fellow politicians or members of the Crisis Staff made any plans to attack Serb villages or persons or seize weaponry from the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the 7th of May, something else happened in 1992. This is when officially the ministry from Sarajevo appointed Omer Filipovic as the commander of the Territorial Defence. And although we did make defence plans, how to defend ourselves -- but at no time did we think about attacking Serbs or to mistreat their civilians. I even said that those that were captured on the 25th in Crljeni, that Omer Filipovic ordered that they should be kept alive, preserved, because he knew what would happen. He said, "Keep them alive. Keep them well. They should not be harmed in any way because we will get for them our people, because now Vinko and Jovo will start to take revenge on our villages." And the evidence that they were treated well was that in Crljeni in the Kljuc municipality there was no massacre, like in other villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So this can perhaps be a thank-you, because we kept these people for them, we kept them alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to deal with that when we get to that in context. But can we now look at a document 88 -- P889.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is objected to as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a report dated the 24th of April, 1992 which has a handwritten number on it and is signed "Milos." No, sorry, you haven't got it. And states: "We have reached an agreement with the chief of the Kljuc SJB that they should take weapons out of the storeroom of the police station all at once and store them in a secure place because there's a real danger of Green Berets launching an attack to seize them. We are proposing that weapons be removed in this manner for tactical reasons so as to avoid alarming the citizens in this area. The Green Berets pose the greatest threat from Vrhpolje and Velagici, where a small area, around 12.500 inhabitants of Muslim background are living." Three questions, please. First: Who was the chief of the Kljuc SJB by April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vinko Kondic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did he become - because you've told us what his job was before - the chief of the SJB, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not be able to remember that, but I think -- I believe it was in 1991. But I cannot give you the exact date. But in any case, after the multi-party elections, he was the secretary of the municipal assembly and he then became chief of police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you know whether or not weapons were removed from the police station?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I presume that the weapons, together with the Territorial Defence weapons, were moved to Kula [Realtime transcript read in error "Kuna"].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry. Whether you presume or not, do you actually know from any information that you got?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my information is that the weapons went. But we neither saw that or heard that. It was hearsay. Nobody knew for sure, not from the SDS. Nobody told us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it alleges that in the Vrhpolje-Velagici area, there were around 12.500 Muslim inhabitants. As far as you're aware, is that a reasonably accurate figure?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe it is. These are two villages wherein that part there are mostly Muslims. For the most part there are Muslims located. Whether it's 12.500 or 10.500, these -- to be sure, we would need documents from the census from 1991 to be absolutely sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Don't worry about that. Yes. Thank you. You can leave that document. And could we now look, please, at Exhibit P890.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, objected to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's handwritten minutes again of the SDS municipal board in Kljuc. And it mentions an assembly being held. And then Vinko Kondic says this: "The situation in Kljuc municipality is unbearably calm. In Bosnian Kljuc, an open conflict broke out between the Serbian Bosnian Kljuc and the official Bosnian Kljuc. We are facing a relatively satisfactory situation in Sanica is probably from the party --" no, the translation is not great on this. "We cannot overcome the situation in a peaceful way. Serbs are the majority population in Kljuc. We control all the important positions. The situation is getting tenser and tenser, and we can hardly avoid war." Now, would you agree with that assessment of Mr. Kondic at that stage on the 29th of April?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vinko Kondic is speaking at this moment the truth. The situation is calm. But he didn't say from whom the war should be avoided, whether it would be from the radical side of the SDS, because they were the ones clamouring for war while the Muslims and Croats were not asking for war. And here what Vinko Kondic says is correct, when he says that is calm. It was calm, apart from the murders that I mentioned earlier and some acts of provocation. There was provocation in order -- so that we would go first, so that we would react.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Then someone called Mirna Jakic, who I don't think we've come across before, says that "Omer is in Sanica preparing the Territorial Defence." First of all, do you know who this lady was?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is Jokic, Marija or perhaps Mira. Because there are Jokic -- Jokic people who are in Sanica. See, Omer married a girl from Sanica just like I did, and each time we went to Sanica, when we went there to see our wives' relatives, it was always commented on among the radical SDS circles saying, "Here they are, the Filipovic brothers are coming organising Green Berets." So we could never move over there without being told that we were doing something against Serbian wishes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was in fact your brother in Sanica preparing the TO? 16 A. Well, I said to start with, we tried to organise ourselves, and Sanica 17 is part of the Bosanski Kljuc municipality, and we attempted to organise 18 the people in Sanica as well. And I stand by that, that we did -- that we did that. We worked on this. How much we succeeded, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we go to an entry apparently made by somebody called Djuro. It could be Jokic as well. It's over on the second page of the translation. He says: "It's taking --" something illegible and then "It's taking some time. Sanski Most is an example of how changes can be implemented in a peaceful way. We in Kljuc have the power, but we don't use it." By the 29th of April, were you in Kljuc aware of what had happened in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Sanski Most the situation was the same as it was in Kljuc, so what Djuro Jokic says, he means how the authority can be used, how the power can be used. He means that we should be slaves, that we should be subordinate to the Serbs. For him that was the power. That's what it meant to have power, while normal democratic power as it was in the rest of Europe, they didn't believe that to be true power because they wanted us to be marked out, to move around with certificates. For them that's what power was. That's what democracy was, the way SDS saw it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then finally somebody called Branko Pucar says, "We should not rule anything out. We must consider what is better for us so as not to go wrong in our estimate. I think it is bad that we have no one from Banja Luka here today to tell us how we should work because they are in touch with the Sarajevo SDS." Do you know who Mr. Branko Pucar was?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I do know Branko Pucar. He was a member of the assembly following the first parliamentary elections. I believe in my assessment he was nuts. In the middle of the summer he was wearing working gloves, and he is one of the people responsible for the massacre in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the place of the massacre.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He always wore the rucksack on his back and he always wore working gloves, not gentleman's gloves but he was wearing working gloves that workers wear when they are carrying out manual work. But he comes from Ribnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The interpreter missed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm just about to ask, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, responsible for the massacre where?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Biljani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now I want you to look, please -- to go in our bundles the very first document on this point of Omer preparing the TO. It's P850.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think this will be the last document, Your Honour. I don't think that it is objected to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first document that we see is a sort of sketch of the SDS municipal civil defence staff and other units. First of all, have you seen sketches like this before, diagrams, I should say?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically this one, I haven't seen this one. But looking at the structure, this is how it was done there. This is a document from the session where a sketch is made or a draft is made and then another official document is later on made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You yourself were involved in the TO. Would you prepare documents like this?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would, because it is always within a structure organisation where you're supposed to make what comes from where. In the army you have a system of subordination, so you have from higher to lower, from greater to smaller. So where things start from, that has to be known.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we look then, please, at the next part of the document, which appears to be headed "Assignments." Under 2, it should be headed "Local board and staff Sanica." "The mobilisation of our forces is to be done on time and at the same time as to give us an advantage over the new Muslim forces in this local area. Under all circumstances and especially at the beginning, rely on the support of the police station and the police force in maintaining order and securing vital property." And then it goes on to, I suppose, lay out a plan of action. And then -- and it's not very clear. I don't know whether you'd be able to read it. But apparently it says: "In Donji Sanica --" and then the translator -- no, and then there's a line. One can see that in the original. "In addition to the staff, have a platoon-size unit whose main task would be a strong attack on Muslim, the enemy's units and use in wider area." Now, do you know whether such a platoon was then stationed in the Donji Sanica area?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not be able to tell you this. Reading through this, Pistanica, Priseka, and Gologlavo, these are all these places that belong to Sanica where the population is of Serb ethnicity, while the actual Sanica downtown is Muslim. Most of them are Muslims, although there are Serbs. But around the village hill -- villages on the hill are mostly Serb inhabitants. So possibly within their plan they had this. But whether I knew about this in this part, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't -- I thought I could finish this document, but in fact there's quite a bit more I need to ask about it, so it may be an appropriate moment. Your Honour, when the witness has left court, can I just raise one matter on timing. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I just wanted to say that this latest -- last document, Mr. Talic's Defence contests it because the date is unknown, the author is unknown. Another matter: On page 64 of the transcript, lines 1, 2, and 3, the witness spoke about a document from February 1992. It was a radio announcement. And what comes out in the transcript is what the witness would have said: [Previous translation continues] ... [In English] "this is one of the many lies." As far as I could understand, in Serbo-Croat I believe that he said this was one of the many false announcements, and this could be quite important for the Defence. It would be good to clarify this. JUDGE AGIUS: Were you following, Mr. Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the announcement is concerned, I didn't say that the announcement was false. I said the dates were false. Madam defence attorney of General Talic, because when the time says that it happened, there was no situation. There were no tense situations where there was a need to read an announcement, while there were announcements of very similar content, countless announcements. And I stand by what I said. But it is the date which is wrong, which is false. That's what I maintain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 79, line 7, Your Honour. When speaking of where weapons were taken, the transcript says Kuna, and the place is actually Kula.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Kula, yes. Point taken. Okay. Mr. Filipovic, we will continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. We will continue tomorrow. You will now be escorted by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted to have a -- because we're flying witnesses in. We've actually got two witnesses here at the moment to follow on for this week, but it's clear that Mr. Filipovic won't finish in chief until Wednesday. Does that mean -- do I take it that cross-examination will last the rest of the week by both sides?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I always get criticised for -- by Ms. Korner for the predictions that I make, so I think I'll not make any more. But it would surprise me if we get beyond this witness this week. But I don't want to get yelled at if I don't have as much cross as I think I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, the two -- the two witnesses who are here will have to stay here now. We didn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There's nothing we can do about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It doesn't -- it wouldn't make sense to send them over and bring them back again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: One of them comes from an exceedingly long way away at vast expense, so he will just have to sit in the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, we wouldn't need any more than those two. If you were thinking of asking more than those two, no, not a chance.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Otherwise -- I'm sorry, but the -- the system is that VWS brings witnesses here for the Monday, Tuesday on the Friday. But if those two witnesses that we have here already will not be heard this week, then we won't get anybody out till next Monday. Yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think it's a fair assessment that we cannot finish -- if we -- if we ever finish -- I mean, if we finish Mr. Filipovic this week at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Because we don't know when the Prosecutor will actually end.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. I will finish. But not until halfway through Wednesday because of the documents I'm taking him through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So that's it. I thank you all. See you tomorrow at the same time. Good evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: at 6.33 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 3rd day of September, 2002, at 2.15 p.m. 24 25
